::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What this lesson is for

In the first lesson you learned to press **Run** and read the answer. Now you will start asking questions
of your data. *Which district landed the most fish? How much was landed last month?*

First, though, it helps to know how your data is arranged:

- What does one line in the table stand for?
- How do the lines fit together?
- What is each column telling you?

That is all this lesson does. Once the shape of the data is clear, the next lessons will make sense. Go
slowly, press **Run** on each box, and remember: **you cannot break anything.**
:::

## Where your data comes from

Your data does not appear from nowhere. Every time an enumerator meets a fisher coming back to a landing
site, they fill in a short survey. It records the date, the landing site, the boat and gear used, how many
people fished, and **what was caught**.

All of those surveys, from every landing site, are collected into **one big table**. That table is your
data. Reading it is simply reading those survey records, stacked one on top of another.

A table has two simple parts:

- a **row** is one line going across. One row is one record.
- a **column** is one heading going down. One column is one piece of information that was recorded, like
  the date or the weight.

The rest of this lesson is about what the rows and columns in *your* table mean.

## A small example to look at

It is easier to see the shape on a small table first. Here is a made-up example — just **two fishing
trips**, with each trip shown in its **own colour**. The fish are simply numbered, **species 1** and so
on, so that nothing here depends on telling one fish from another.

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>survey_id</th><th>trip_id</th><th>landing_date</th><th>gaul_2_name</th><th>gear</th><th>catch_taxon</th><th>catch_kg</th><th>n_catch</th><th>tot_catch_kg</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 1</td><td>12</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 2</td><td>5</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 3</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-b"><td>survey_2</td><td>trip_2</td><td>2024-01-06</td><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>species 1</td><td>8</td><td>2</td><td>14</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-b"><td>survey_2</td><td>trip_2</td><td>2024-01-06</td><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>species 2</td><td>6</td><td>2</td><td>14</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>

<p class="diagram-legend"><span class="grp-a"></span> Trip 1 &nbsp;&nbsp; <span class="grp-b"></span> Trip 2</p>
```

Take a moment to read it. Notice that some things **repeat** down the table while others **change** on
every line. We will come back to that, because it is the key to understanding your data.

The headings are the **real headings from your own data**. Here is that same little table inside R, so we
can work with it. This box runs on its own when the page opens — you do not have to do anything yet.

{{< include _slow-start-notice.qmd >}}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# The same five rows as the coloured table above.
example <- data.frame(
  survey_id    = c("survey_1", "survey_1", "survey_1", "survey_2", "survey_2"),
  trip_id      = c("trip_1", "trip_1", "trip_1", "trip_2", "trip_2"),
  landing_date = c("2024-01-05", "2024-01-05", "2024-01-05", "2024-01-06", "2024-01-06"),
  gaul_2_name  = c("Shimoni", "Shimoni", "Shimoni", "Vanga", "Vanga"),
  gear         = c("hand line", "hand line", "hand line", "gillnet", "gillnet"),
  catch_taxon  = c("species 1", "species 2", "species 3", "species 1", "species 2"),
  catch_kg     = c(12, 5, 3, 8, 6),
  n_catch      = c(3, 3, 3, 2, 2),
  tot_catch_kg = c(20, 20, 20, 14, 14)
)

example
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** the same **5 rows** as the coloured table. You can slide it sideways to see all
the columns.
:::

## What one row means

Look at the very first line. It is one **catch**: *species 1, 12 kg*. The second line is another catch:
*species 2, 5 kg*.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Each row is one catch — one kind of fish from one trip.**
:::

This is the first thing to hold on to. A row is **not** a whole trip, and it is **not** one fisher. It
is one *kind of fish* that was recorded. So if a single trip brought back three kinds of fish, that
trip fills **three rows**.

## How the rows fit into trips

You may have noticed something that confuses almost everyone at first. The same district, the same date
and the same `trip_id` appear on several lines.

Nothing is wrong. This is exactly how the data is meant to look.

The reason is simple. **One fishing trip usually brings back more than one kind of fish.**

Each trip is given an identity code, called **`trip_id`**. Every kind of fish from that trip gets its own
row, and they all carry the **same** `trip_id`. That shared code is how you know which rows belong to the
same trip. (`survey_id` works the same way. It names the survey the record came from.)

In the example, `trip_1` brought back three kinds of fish, so it fills three rows. `trip_2` brought back
two, so it fills two rows. Here is that first trip drawn as a picture:

```{=html}
<svg class="diagram diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 640 210" role="img" aria-label="One trip with three catches">
  <rect class="grp-a" x="10" y="75" width="175" height="60" rx="8"/>
  <text x="97" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">Trip  trip_1</text>
  <text x="97" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12">Shimoni &#183; 5 Jan</text>
  <path class="link" d="M185 105 C 235 105 235 35 285 35"/>
  <path class="link" d="M185 105 H 285"/>
  <path class="link" d="M185 105 C 235 105 235 175 285 175"/>
  <rect class="row-box" x="285" y="15"  width="345" height="40" rx="6"/><text x="300" y="40" font-size="13">species 1 &#8212; 12 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan class="row-label">row 1</tspan></text>
  <rect class="row-box" x="285" y="85"  width="345" height="40" rx="6"/><text x="300" y="110" font-size="13">species 2 &#8212; 5 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan class="row-label">row 2</tspan></text>
  <rect class="row-box" x="285" y="155" width="345" height="40" rx="6"/><text x="300" y="180" font-size="13">species 3 &#8212; 3 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan class="row-label">row 3</tspan></text>
</svg>
```

[One trip, three kinds of fish → three rows, all sharing `trip_id = trip_1`.]{.diagram-caption}

The column **`n_catch`** writes that number down for you: it is **how many kinds of catch the trip
recorded**. You don't have to take it on trust — you can count the rows for each trip yourself. Press
**Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Count how many rows carry each trip_id.
table(example$trip_id)
```

The result shows `trip_1  3` and `trip_2  2`. Three rows for the first trip, two for the second. That
matches the `n_catch` column exactly.

Counting how often something appears is already a useful skill, and you will use it again later.

## Two kinds of columns

Now look across the columns. Once you see it, you cannot un-see it: the columns fall into **two groups**.
(Here the colours mark the **two kinds of columns** — not the trips as before.)

```{=html}
<div class="col-groups">
  <div class="about-trip">
    <strong>About the trip</strong> <span class="text-secondary">(same on every row)</span><br>
    <code>landing_date</code>, <code>gaul_2_name</code>, <code>gear</code>, <code>n_fishers</code>, <code>tot_catch_kg</code> &#8230;
  </div>
  <div class="about-catch">
    <strong>About each catch</strong> <span class="text-secondary">(changes on each row)</span><br>
    <code>catch_taxon</code>, <code>catch_kg</code>, <code>length_cm</code>, <code>catch_price</code>
  </div>
</div>
```

Some columns describe the **whole trip**. The trip happened once, so these are the **same on every row of
that trip**. They include `landing_date`, `gaul_2_name`, `gear`, and `tot_catch_kg`, the **total** weight
the trip brought in.

Other columns describe **each catch on its own**, so they **change from row to row**. They include
`catch_taxon` and `catch_kg`, the weight of that **one** kind of fish.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
This difference matters in real work.

- **`tot_catch_kg`** is the whole trip's weight.
- **`catch_kg`** is one kind of fish's weight.

If you added up `tot_catch_kg` over every row, you would count the same trip several times. The number
would come out far too big. So use `tot_catch_kg` for a trip total, and `catch_kg` for a single catch.
:::

You do not need to memorise the columns. The next lessons introduce them one at a time. For now, just hold
three things in your head:

- **A row is one catch.**
- **Rows group into trips.**
- **Every column is either about the trip or about the catch.**

## Looking at your own data

You now know the shape. Now look at **your real landing records** in the same kind of table. They were
fetched for you when this page opened:

{{< include _landings-panel.qmd >}}

Your records are held under the name **`landings`**. Press **Run** to see them:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
landings
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
This is your real data, and it has the **same shape** as the small example. Try typing the name of your
district, or a kind of fish, into the **search box** — or click a column heading to **sort**. Looking
around like this is the best way to get a feel for what you actually have.
:::

## How big is your data

Two simple questions help you get your bearings: **how many records** do you have, and **how many
columns** describe each one? Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
nrow(landings)   # number of records (rows)
ncol(landings)   # number of columns
```

The first number is how many catch records you hold, often many thousands. The second is how many pieces
of information are kept about each catch.

That is far more than you could read by eye in a spreadsheet. This is exactly why we use R. It can look
through all of it for you in a moment, which is what the next lessons will do.

## What each column means

Finally, let's see the columns by name. Press **Run** to list them:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
names(landings)
```

These are the headings in your table. Below is what the main ones mean, grouped the same way we saw
above. **Keep this nearby. It is the dictionary for your data.**

{{< include _data-dictionary.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two things that look different in your real table

The **column headings** are the same as the small example, so what you practised will work here. But two
of the **values** look different, and it is worth knowing why before you go on.

- **The fish is a code.** In your real data `catch_taxon` holds a short code (for example `SKJ`, which
  means skipjack tuna), not a plain name. The `scientific_name` column gives its full name. In the small
  example we simply wrote *species 1*, *species 2* and *species 3*, so that nothing you practised
  depended on knowing which fish is which.
- **`gaul_2_name` is the district, not the landing site.** The odd name comes from an international list
  of areas. Your table records the **district** a record belongs to, not the individual beach or jetty.
:::

## What you have learned

You can now read the shape of your data:

- a **row** is one catch — one kind of fish from one trip;
- rows belong together when they share a **`trip_id`**, and **`n_catch`** says how many a trip had;
- every column is either **about the trip** (the same on every row) or **about each catch** (different on each row);
- your real data has this same shape — just much bigger.

That is the foundation. In the next lesson you will start to **find the rows you need**. For example,
only the landings from your district, or only one month.
